claims.text: Tribo-corrosion resistance in high-entropy alloys is governed by a dense, stable oxide layer formed through controlled thermal-shock annealing.
The oxide layer reduces wear by providing a hard, low-friction interface.
The oxide layer limits corrosion by acting as a barrier to aggressive species.
An untreated high-entropy-alloy surface may possess a native, non-optimized oxide layer.
Thermal-shock annealing can produce a dense and stable oxide film on an HEA surface.
Annealing an AlCrTiZrMo HEA film at 800 °C for 1 hour forms a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer.
The thermally formed oxide resists surface damage and lowers friction.
The dense oxide prevents continued oxidation.
Relative to an untreated matched baseline, thermal-shock annealing will lower the overall tribo-corrosion degradation rate.
Relative to an untreated matched baseline, thermal-shock annealing will lower the wear rate.
Relative to an untreated matched baseline, thermal-shock annealing will lower the corrosion current.
The protective effect should hold under moderate tribological and corrosive conditions while the oxide remains intact.
Extremely high mechanical loads or mechanical disruption of the oxide should diminish the coupled protective effect.
The proposed comparison uses identical sliding tests in 3.5% NaCl, differing only in whether thermal-shock annealing is applied.
Wear rate, corrosion current density, and oxide-layer integrity are measurable outcomes for the controlled comparison.
Failure of annealed samples to show statistically significant reductions in both wear rate and corrosion current relative to the untreated control would falsify the prediction.
A correlation between degradation and oxide-layer breakdown would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism and boundary predict that oxide breakdown should coincide with increased degradation and loss of protection. Therefore, observing degradation correlate with oxide breakdown would support the proposed mechanism rather than falsify it.
